note: Source's conditional 'if men believe' became a flat assertion and 'necessarily' was dropped.
replacement: The principle of utility has all the sanctions that belong to any other system of morals, or at least there is no reason why it might not have them. Those sanctions are either external or internal. I need not speak at any length of the external sanctions. They are the hope of favor and the fear of displeasure from our fellow creatures or from the Ruler of the Universe. Along with these go whatever sympathy or affection we may have for our fellow creatures, or love and awe of Him, which incline us to do His will independently of selfish consequences. There is plainly no reason why all these motives for observance should not attach themselves to the utilitarian morality as completely and as powerfully as to any other. Indeed, those that concern our fellow creatures are sure to do so in proportion to the amount of general intelligence. For whether or not there is any other ground of moral obligation than the general happiness, men do desire happiness. However imperfect their own practice may be, they desire and commend all conduct in others toward themselves by which they think their happiness is promoted. As for the religious motive, if men believe in the goodness of God, as most profess to do, then those who think that conduciveness to the general happiness is the essence of good, or even only its criterion, must necessarily believe that it is also what God approves. So the whole force of external reward and punishment, whether physical or moral, and whether it comes from God or from our fellow men, becomes available to enforce the utilitarian morality, in proportion as that morality is recognized. The same holds for all the disinterested devotion to either that human nature admits of. And the more education and general cultivation are bent to this purpose, the more powerful that force becomes.

note: 'What opinion they like' adds a flippant sense and the concession 'however they may believe (as they do)' was flattened.
replacement: But does the utilitarian doctrine deny that people desire virtue? Does it maintain that virtue is not a thing to be desired? The very reverse. It maintains that virtue is to be desired, and desired disinterestedly, for itself. Utilitarian moralists may hold any opinion about the original conditions that make virtue what it is. They may believe (as they do) that actions and dispositions are virtuous only because they promote some end other than virtue. Yet once this is granted, and once such considerations have settled what _is_ virtuous, they do two things. First, they put virtue at the very head of the things that are good as means to the ultimate end. Second, they recognize as a psychological fact that virtue may be, for the individual, a good in itself, with no looking to any end beyond it. They hold that the mind is not in a right state, not in a state conformable to Utility, not in the state most conducive to the general happiness, unless it loves virtue in this manner, as a thing desirable in itself. This holds even if, in the individual instance, virtue does not produce the other desirable consequences it tends to produce, and on account of which it is held to be virtue. This opinion is not in the smallest degree a departure from the Happiness principle. Happiness has very various ingredients, and each of them is desirable in itself, not merely when counted as swelling an aggregate. The principle of utility does not mean that a given pleasure, such as music, or a given exemption from pain, such as health, should be looked on as a means to some collective something called happiness, and desired on that account. They are desired and desirable in and for themselves. Besides being means, they are a part of the end. On the utilitarian doctrine, virtue is not naturally and originally part of the end, but it is capable of becoming so. In those who love it disinterestedly it has become so. They desire and cherish it not as a means to happiness but as a part of their happiness.
